name: Chronic rhinosinusitis
aliases: chronic rhinosinusitis with or without nasal polyps

reference.source: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
clinicalPearls: Chronic rhinosinusitis is symptomatic inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses persisting for at least twelve weeks
Diagnosis requires two or more cardinal symptoms, at least one being nasal blockage or nasal discharge, alongside facial pressure/pain or reduction in sense of smell
It is broadly classified into disease with nasal polyps and disease without polyps, which differ in inflammatory pattern and treatment response
Objective evidence of inflammation on nasal endoscopy or CT is needed to confirm the diagnosis, as symptoms alone are non-specific
Obstruction of the osteomeatal complex impairing sinus ventilation and mucociliary clearance is central to the disease
Contributing factors include allergy, asthma, aspirin sensitivity, structural abnormalities, biofilms and, in some cases, fungal disease and immune deficiency
First-line treatment is medical, centred on saline irrigation and topical intranasal corticosteroids, with other measures directed at the underlying driver
Functional endoscopic sinus surgery is reserved for disease that fails maximal medical therapy or where complications or specific anatomy demand it
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic rhinosinusitis reflects a persistent inflammatory process of the sinonasal mucosa rather than simple ongoing infection. Anatomical narrowing or mucosal swelling at the osteomeatal complex obstructs sinus outflow, disrupting ventilation and mucociliary clearance so that secretions stagnate and mucosal inflammation is perpetuated. Host factors (allergy, asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, immune dysfunction, ciliary disorders) and environmental factors (microbial biofilms, fungi, irritants) drive different inflammatory endotypes; polypoid disease is often eosinophilic and type 2 driven, whereas non-polypoid disease tends to be more neutrophilic. Chronic inflammation causes mucosal oedema, polyp formation and epithelial remodelling that further obstruct drainage, creating a self-sustaining cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis and other granulomatous diseases
Cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea mimicking chronic discharge
Sinonasal neoplasm, especially with unilateral disease
additionalInvestigations: Nasal endoscopy to document mucopus, oedema and polyps
CT of the paranasal sinuses to assess extent and osteomeatal complex anatomy
Allergy testing where an allergic component is suspected
Nasal or sinus swab for culture in resistant or complicated cases
Biopsy of atypical or unilateral lesions to exclude neoplasia or granulomatous disease
Investigations for immune deficiency or ciliary dysfunction in recalcitrant disease
redFlags: Strictly unilateral symptoms or bloody discharge suggesting neoplasm
Periorbital swelling, proptosis, visual disturbance or ophthalmoplegia indicating orbital complication (an emergency)
Severe headache, high fever, neck stiffness or neurological signs suggesting intracranial spread
Clear watery rhinorrhoea after trauma or surgery suggesting a cerebrospinal fluid leak
Rapidly progressive symptoms with facial numbness or palatal changes in an immunocompromised patient (invasive fungal disease)
reference.prognosis: Most patients achieve good symptom control with appropriate medical therapy and, where needed, surgery, but the condition is often chronic and relapsing, particularly the polypoid, eosinophilic and aspirin-sensitive forms, which frequently recur and may require long-term treatment including biologics.
pitfalls: Diagnosing chronic rhinosinusitis on symptoms alone without objective endoscopic or CT confirmation
Overlooking a unilateral lesion that could be a tumour
Treating repeatedly with antibiotics rather than addressing the underlying inflammatory driver
Missing orbital or intracranial complications during an acute exacerbation
Failing to consider allergy, asthma or immune deficiency in recurrent disease
references: Dhingra, Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat
management: Intranasal corticosteroids combined with saline nasal irrigation as the mainstay of medical therapy
Short courses of oral corticosteroids for severe polyposis or exacerbations
Treatment of underlying drivers, including allergy control and asthma management, with aspirin desensitisation in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease
Biologic therapy such as dupilumab, omalizumab or mepolizumab for severe eosinophilic polypoid disease
Antibiotics reserved for acute bacterial exacerbations, with a macrolide considered in selected non-eosinophilic disease
Functional endoscopic sinus surgery for disease refractory to optimised medical therapy
Investigation and management of immunodeficiency or ciliary dysfunction in recalcitrant cases
Long-term topical therapy with endoscopic surveillance given the relapsing course
